description: 100 deep logical questions on polymorphism in Python OOP

questions.answer:
duck quack
person quacking
This is duck typing: make_noise never checks the declared or runtime type of `thing`; it only calls `thing.quack()` at the last moment. As long as an object exposes a callable quack attribute, the function accepts it, so both Duck and Person work despite having no common base class.

3
len(x) is syntactic sugar for calling the protocol method x.__len__(). Built-in len() looks up __len__ in the instance's type and requires it to return a non-negative integer; here it delegates to the list's own length of 3.

questions.question:
What error, if any, does this raise and why?
```python
class Squad:
    def __init__(self, members):
        self.members = members
print(len(Squad([1, 2])))
```
questions.answer:
TypeError: object of type 'Squad' has no len()
len() goes through CPython's C-level tp_as_sequence peephole and only accepts a __len__ method. Unlike iteration, it does NOT fall back to __getitem__; since Squad defines neither, the TypeError fires even though the object holds a list whose length could be inferred.

questions.question:
Fill in the missing dunder so this prints `Point(3)` three times. Then predict the output:
```python
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x):
        self.x = x
    def ____(self):
        return f'Point({self.x})'
p = Point(3)
print(p)
print(str(p))
print(repr(p))
```
questions.answer:
Fill in `__repr__`. Output:
Point(3)
Point(3)
Point(3)
When __str__ is missing, str() and print() fall back to __repr__, so all three calls resolve to the same source. Defining __repr__ alone is enough to give the object a readable textual form everywhere.

[A-repr, <__main__.B object at 0x...>]
A-repr
B-str
Containers format each element with repr(), so B() inside the list shows the default object repr because B never defines __repr__; A() shows 'A-repr'. Standalone print() calls str(), which prefers __str__ (B) and falls back to __repr__ (A). The two dunders are dispatched in different contexts.

3
<__main__.Vector object at 0x...>
a + b is dispatched as type(a).__add__(a, b), so the left operand's __add__ builds a new Vector(3), and the first print shows 3. The second line prints the new object, but Vector defines neither __repr__ nor __str__, so repr falls back to object's identity-based default.

A homogeneous Money + Money uses the forward __add__ directly and returns Money(3).

Any rich comparison that cannot be done forwards is attempted with swapped operands before raising TypeError.

unhashable type: 'Plate'
Defining __eq__ without also defining __hash__ implicitly sets the class attribute __hash__ to None. This makes instances unhashable by design - they can no longer be set elements or dict keys - and hash(Plate(1)) raises TypeError. Re-add __hash__ only when equal objects must hash equally.

Add `def __hash__(self): return hash(self.v)` to Key.
Then the print shows 1. A dict hashes keys first and only then applies __eq__ to resolve hash collisions; once __eq__ is defined without __hash__, the class is unhashable and even constructing the dict from Key('a') raises TypeError. Equal objects must also produce equal hashes, which hash(self.v) guarantees for equal strings.

HELLO!
LoudGreeter overrides greet, but the zero-argument super() forwards the call to the next class in the instance's MRO after LoudGreeter - here Greeter - whose greet returns 'Hello'. The subclass then uppercases and appends '!' before returning the joined result.

DBCA
super() walks a cooperative chain, not just the direct parent. C3 linearization orders D, B, C, A (D inherits B before C, and both share A), so D calls B.f, B chains to C.f, C chains to A.f, and the prefix concatenation produces 'DBCA'.

Base init
Right init
Left init
Child init
The zero-argument super() in the diamond follows the MRO Child, Left, Right, Base. Each __init__ defers its own print until after super().__init__() returns, so control sinks to Base first and boomerangs back up: Base, then Right, then Left, and finally Child. This is the cooperative super() pattern in action.

swimming

20
len() finds the dedicated __len__ protocol and returns 3. Since Seq defines no __iter__, CPython falls back to the sequence protocol: list(s) repeatedly calls __getitem__ with index 0, 1, 2 and stops at IndexError, collecting [10, 20, 30]. questions.question:
What error does this raise and why?
```python
class Bad:
    def __iter__(self):
        return [1, 2, 3]
print(list(Bad()))
```
questions.answer:
TypeError: iter() returned non-iterator of type 'list'
__iter__ must hand back an object that itself implements the iterator protocol (a __next__ method). A plain list is a re-iterable container, not an iterator, so CPython rejects the return value at the C level before list() can digest it. Returning self from __iter__ is the canonical fix.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
```python
class NumSet:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
    def __contains__(self, x):
        return 0 <= x < self.n
r = NumSet(5)
print(3 in r)
print(7 in r)
```
questions.answer:
True
False
The `in` operator dispatches to type(r).__contains__(r, 3); the predicate 0 <= 3 < 5 is True, while 0 <= 7 < 5 is False. __contains__ takes priority during membership tests; it is only skipped in favor of __iter__ or __getitem__ when the method is absent.

True
False
R defines no __contains__, so `in` falls back to iterating via the sequence protocol: __getitem__(0), __getitem__(1), ... until IndexError. The yielded values are 0, 10, 20 - 20 matches, 99 never appears. The outward polymorphism is identical to a real container, even though membership is ultimately a linear scan.

False True True
Truthiness is the polymorphic protocol bool(): type(A) declares __bool__ returning False, so A is falsy. B provides only __len__, so CPython falls back to it and treats a length of 5 as truthy. C has neither dunder, so it defaults to the always-truthy object identity rule.

default:secret
default:missing
__getattribute__ is consulted for every attribute access; for 'secret' it raises AttributeError, and that exception hands control to the fallback hook __getattr__, which fabricates the string. 'missing' never reaches __getattribute__'s happy path for a real attribute but is caught by the same fallback. Only when __getattribute__ raises AttributeError does __getattr__ run.

Goblin
Dragon
A classmethod receives the actual invoking class; Enemy.spawn calls cls() with cls bound to Goblin or Dragon respectively. Allowing any class to be passed and invoking its spawn makes teleport polymorphic over enemy classes without a switch statement, using late-bound cls to construct the right kind.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
```python
class Counter:
    def total(self):
        return 10
c = Counter()
print(c.total())
c.total = 99
print(c.total)
print(Counter.total(c))
```
questions.answer:
10
99
10
c.total() first dispatches to the bound method and prints 10. Assigning c.total = 99 installs an instance attribute that shadows the class method for instance access, so print(c.total) shows the int 99 without calling anything. Counter.total(c) reaches the class attribute directly and calls the original function with c as self, restoring 10.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
```python
class Person:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name, self.age = name, age
    def __repr__(self):
        return self.name
people = [Person('bob', 30), Person('alice', 25), Person('carol', 25)]
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: p.age))
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: (p.age, p.name)))
```
questions.answer:
[alice, carol, bob]
[alice, carol, bob]
sorted() never inspects the objects' types; it extracts the key from each element by calling the lambda and sorts those keys. With the bare age key both Person(25) entries are stable in input order (alice, carol). The tuple key (age, name) ties-broken by name produces the same order because alice < carol; duck typing lets one sort routine handle any object exposing the needed attributes.

[1, 2, 3]
With no key argument, sort falls back to comparing elements directly, dispatching to Grade.__lt__ for each pair. Only __lt__ is needed for Timsort's comparisons, and the repr gives the readable [1, 2, 3] output; the objects themselves never leave their class.

Money(43)
sum() accumulates with + starting from the integer 0 even for non-numeric types. The first addition 0 + Money(1) fails in int.__add__, bounces into Money.__radd__, and every subsequent step is a forward Money + Money; without __radd__ the very first element would raise TypeError instead.

questions.question:
What error does this raise and why?
```python
class Odd:
    def __str__(self):
        return 123
print(f'{Odd()}')
```
questions.answer:
TypeError: __str__ returned non-string (type int)
Both f-string formatting and str() first call __str__ and then demand the precise str result. Returning any other type, here the int 123, is rejected with a TypeError thrown by the format slot. repr() remains unaffected and would still succeed separately.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
```python
class Money:
    def __init__(self, v):
        self.v = v
    def __format__(self, spec):
        return f'${self.v:.{spec}f}' if spec else f'${self.v}'
m = Money(12.345)
print(f'{m}')
print(f'{m:2}')
```
questions.answer:
$12.345
$12.35
An f-string passes the format specification (the text after the colon, else '') straight to the object's __format__. The empty spec takes the plain branch and yields $12.345; the spec '2' is spliced into the float mini-spec to round to two decimals, $12.35.

'float' object cannot be interpreted as an integer
The builtin len() validates the return of __len__ through the integer conversion machinery, so a float result is rejected before it can propagate. A correct __len__ must yield a non-negative int (or an object with __index__), even though len() affects truthiness and iteration behavior too.

unsupported operand type(s) for *: 'Weird' and 'int'
__index__ is the protocol for integer-lookalike operations (indexing, slicing, bin/hex/oct, range), NOT for arithmetic. Multiplication dispatches to __mul__/__rmul__; neither exists, so the left slot fails, the type lookup yields no reflected method, and the expression collapses to TypeError. Adding __mul__ would fix it.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
```python
class Idx:
    def __index__(self):
        return 2
i = Idx()
print([10, 20, 30, 40][i])
print(list(range(Idx())))
```
questions.answer:
30
[0, 1]
Subscripting and range() demand an integral index, resolved via the __index__ protocol rather than __int__ or float conversion. The list lookup converts i to 2 and pulls 30; range(Idx()) respects its new-style integer conversion to produce 0 and 1. This lets custom types behave like integers wherever positions are required.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
```python
class F(float):
    def __mul__(self, other):
        return F(float(self) * float(other))
f = F(2.5)
a = f * 3
b = 3 * f
print(a, type(a).__name__)
print(b, type(b).__name__)
```
questions.answer:
7.5 F
7.5 float
When the left operand is the float subclass, its overridden __mul__ runs and the result is F. When int is on the left, int.__mul__ successfully performs the int-float coercion before any subclass hook is consulted, so the reflected F.__rmul__ is never reached and a plain float comes back. Dispatch symmetry is therefore not guaranteed for mixed built-in arithmetic.

5 TinyInt
5 int
TinyInt on the left gets first crack, its __add__ wraps the sum back into TinyInt, and print shows '5 TinyInt'. With int on the left, int.__add__ accepts the TinyInt operand natively during the built-in numeric path and returns an ordinary int 5; the reflected right-side method is only an option if the base type reports NotImplemented.

30
[1, 2]
__getitem__ is handed either a plain int or a slice object depending on the subscript syntax. The integer branch transforms index -1 into 3 * 10 = 30, while slice objects are detected with isinstance and passed straight to the underlying list so l[0:2] is [1, 2]. The single protocol entry point dispatches on the key's own type.

zed
KeyError
Subscript assignment translates to __setitem__, subscript read to __getitem__, and `del b[k]` to __delitem__. After deletion the underlying dict is empty, so __getitem__ re-raises the dict's KeyError and the except block emits 'KeyError'. The same bracket syntax is polymorphic across all three verbs.

8
Dictionary dispatch treats operation names as polymorphic selectors: run looks up a name in the mapping and uniformly invokes whatever callable it finds. This avoids long chains of if/elif branches and makes it trivial to append new strategies. The lambdas share one calling convention, so run stays fixed while behavior varies behind the key.

10
25
True
Objects that implement __call__ become instances that are also callable, so they can be passed wherever a plain function is expected and invoked with the same () syntax. callable() confirms this by reporting True. The apply helper is stimulus-agnostic: it never distinguishes functions from callable objects.

log: enter
5
The decorator @logged rewires the name total onto a logged instance whose __init__ captured the original function. Calling total(2, 3) therefore triggers logged.__call__, which logs and then delegates to the stored function. Because __call__ duck-types as a callable, the decorated result is transparently usable exactly like the original function.

[1, 0]
[]
The design is a self-iterator: __iter__ returns self and __next__ maintains state on the same object, so after the first list(r) the counter is exhausted and the second attempt immediately raises StopIteration. Fix by keeping __iter__ stateless - e.g. have it return `iter(range(self.n))` or reset counter - so each iteration starts fresh and the object is re-iterable.

Base
AttributeError
The two-argument form super(Sub, s) starts the MRO search immediately after Sub on s's type chain, landing on Base.who and printing 'Base'. super(Base, s) begins after Base, and with only object left in the MRO there is no who attribute, so the call raises AttributeError.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
```python
class Base:
    pass
class Child(Base):
    pass
c = Child()
print(isinstance(c, Base))
print(isinstance(c, Child))
print(issubclass(Child, Base))
print(isinstance(Base, Child))
print(isinstance(c, (Base, str)))
```
questions.answer:
True
True
True
False
True
isinstance answers 'is this object an instance of that class, any of its subclasses, or a registered virtual subclass', while issubclass asks about inheritance between classes themselves. Base is a class, never an instance of Child, hence False. A tuple in the second argument is an OR over the listed types, so Child instance qualifies through Base.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
```python
class Tag:
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return True
print(Tag() != Tag())
print(Tag() != 5)
```
questions.answer:
False
False
!= has its own dunder __ne__, but when a class omits it the default object.__ne__ simply negates the result of __eq__. Both comparisons invoke the unconditional __eq__, which returns True, so both != checks report False regardless of the other operand's type.

cannot use 'Blob' as a set element (unhashable type: 'Blob')
Defining __eq__ without __hash__ silently laminates the class as unhashable (__hash__ = None). Set and dict operations hash every member first, so the TypeError fires before __eq__ can ever run, even though the two instances would compare equal. Restore a matching __hash__ to satisfy both protocols.

Fill in `NotImplemented`. Then: TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'Num' and 'int', followed by Num(3). Returning NotImplemented tells the runtime 'I cannot combine with this type, try the right operand's reflected method'. For Num(2) + 1 that is int.__radd__, which also refuses Num, so the whole operation degrades to TypeError; for 1 + Num(2) the reflected Num.__radd__ rescues the sum into Num(3).

212 degrees
212 degrees
A property is a data descriptor, so t.temp transparently executes the getter for whichever class supplies it. The report function only demands the temp attribute and never cares about the concrete type, giving it full duck-typed polymorphism without shared inheritance. Both temperature classes expose the identical attribute protocol and therefore produce the same output.

questions.question: Predict the error. class Vec: def __init__(self, x, y): self.x, self.y = x, y / def __add__(self, other): return Vec(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y). v = Vec(1, 2); then evaluate v + (3, 4). What happens, and what is the fix?
questions.answer: AttributeError: 'tuple' object has no attribute 'x'. Vec.__add__ blindly reads other.x, but the right operand is a plain tuple, and Python never falls back to a reflected operation because __add__ raised instead of returning NotImplemented. Fix: make __add__ return NotImplemented for unknown types and add __radd__(self, other) that unpacks tuples, e.g. def __radd__(self, other): return Vec(other[0] + self.x, other[1] + self.y). Only when the left operator returns NotImplemented does Python consult the right operand's reflected methods.

questions.question: Predict the output. class SuperNum: / def __radd__(self, other): return f'{other} + radd'. print(1 + SuperNum())
questions.answer: 1 + radd. For 1 + obj, Python first tries int.__add__(1, SuperNum()), which does not know how to combine with this class and returns NotImplemented. Python then falls back to the reflected SuperNum.__radd__(1), whose other receives the int, producing '1 + radd'. This right-hand dispatch is what lets you support int + MyClass without touching int.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Left: def __add__(self, other): return 'left'. class Right: def __radd__(self, other): return 'right'. print(Left() + Right())
questions.answer: left. For a normal binary operation the left operand is always consulted first; only if Left.__add__ is missing or explicitly returns NotImplemented does Python try Right.__radd__. Both methods exist here, but Left.__add__ is tried first and returns 'left', so the reflected method is never reached. This is the symmetric-dispatch priority rule: forward before reflected, and left operand before right operand when both define the same slot.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Great: / def __init__(self): self.nums = [] / def __iadd__(self, other): self.nums.append(other); return self. x = Great(); y = x; x += 10; print(y.nums)
questions.answer: [10]. The augmented assignment invokes x.__iadd__(10), which mutates the shared self.nums list in place and returns self, and Python rebinds x to that returned object. Because x and y alias the same instance, y sees the appended 10. The key point: __iadd__ must return the object to keep the target bound to the (possibly mutated) instance; returning a copy would break aliasing assumptions.

questions.question: Find the bug. class Weird: / def __init__(self, v): self.v = v / def __iadd__(self, other): self.v += other  # note: no return. a = Weird(1); a += 1; print(a.v). Why does this crash?
questions.answer: AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'v'. The augmented assignment operator does not ignore the return value of __iadd__: after calling it, a is rebinding to whatever __iadd__ returned, which is None because no return statement is present. The print then reads None.v. Fix: return self (or return the new value) from __iadd__. The invocation-time contract is that Python uses the method's return value, regardless of any in-place side effect.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Point: / def __init__(self, x): self.x = x / def __add__(self, other): return Point(self.x + other). q = Point(4); r = q; q += 3; print(r.x, q.x)
questions.answer: 4 7. Point defines no __iadd__, so q += 3 falls back to q = q + 3, i.e. it calls Point.__add__(q, 3), which builds a brand-new Point(7), and q is rebound to it. The original instance still reachable through r keeps x = 4. Contrast this with an __iadd__ implementation that mutates and returns self: there every alias would observe 7. This fallback means += is semantics-preserving even for immutable-ish classes.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Num: / def __init__(self, v): self.v = v / def __iadd__(self, o): return self.v + o. n = Num(3); n += 4; print(n, type(n).__name__)
questions.answer: 7 int. __iadd__ may legally return any object at all; Python does not require it to return the same type or even an instance of the class. Here __iadd__ returns a plain int 7, and the += statement rebinds n to that int. This shows why in-place operators are ultimately just 'call a dunder and rebind to its return value', which is why libraries returning NotImplemented deliberately break the chain.

questions.question: Predict the error. class NoNeg: pass. What happens when you evaluate -NoNeg()?
questions.answer: TypeError: bad operand type for unary -: 'NoNeg'. Python looks up the nb_negative slot (the __neg__ dunder); since the class defines no __neg__ (and no __pos__/__abs__ equivalents to fall back on for sign), there is nothing to dispatch to, so a TypeError is raised. Every unary numeric operator in PyNumber_Negative requires its slot: -x needs __neg__, abs(x) needs __abs__, ~x needs __invert__, and none of them is synthesized from the others.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Empty: / def __len__(self): return 0. print(bool(Empty()), not Empty())
questions.answer: False True. bool(x) first consults __bool__; since Empty lacks it, Python falls back to __len__ and treats a non-zero length as true, zero length as false. Empty() truthiness therefore equals 0, so bool() is False and not Empty() is True. This __len__ fallback is why any class implementing the sequence protocol automatically gains meaningful truthiness for free.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Mix: / def __bool__(self): return False / def __len__(self): return 5. print(bool(Mix()))
questions.answer: False. Precedence rule: __bool__ wins whenever it is defined, before __len__ is ever consulted, so the len of 5 is irrelevant. The bool slot is checked first; only if it is absent does PbPyNumber_True follow the __len__ path. Here __bool__ explicitly returns False, so all truthiness evaluations of Mix() short-circuit to False.

questions.question: Predict the output. class SameSame: / def __eq__(self, other): return 'same'. print(SameSame() == SameSame())
questions.answer: same. Rich comparison operators are dispatched through the __eq__ slot and their result is returned verbatim; unlike < and >, == performs no coercion of the returned value to bool in pure-Python terms when you print it. So a non-bool literal like the string 'same' propagates straight out of the == expression. (Beware: using this == result in an if or and/or works because Python then applies truthiness to whatever was returned.)

questions.question: Predict the output. class R: / def __eq__(self, other): return 'yes'. print(R() != R())
questions.answer: False. R defines no __ne__, so != is computed from ==: R() == R() returns 'yes' (truthy) and the != operator returns the boolean negation of that truthiness, i.e. False. This is why a class that only overrides __eq__ still behaves correctly with !=. If __eq__ had returned NotImplemented, != would have continued to the reflected side and eventually defaulted to identity/inverse semantics.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Price: / def __init__(self, v): self.v = v / def __eq__(self, o): return self.v == o.v. p1, p2 = Price(1), Price(2); print(p1 == p2, p1 != p2)
questions.answer: False True. __eq__ compares value fields, so Price(1) is not equal to Price(2). The != operator has no __ne__ of its own and is synthesized as the negation of the value-level __eq__ result, so it returns True. The critical subtlety: even if __eq__ returned a falsy-but-not-None sentinel, != would invert that, so the two operators stay logically consistent.

questions.question: Predict the error. class F: / def __lt__(self, o): return True. What happens for 5 < F()?
questions.answer: TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'F'. int.__lt__(5, F()) returns NotImplemented, so Python tries the reflected F().__gt__(5); F defines no __gt__ and returns NotImplemented as well, so the comparison fails with a TypeError. Merely defining __lt__ on one operand is not enough when the other operand is the one being compared; both sides of the < relation must be supported somewhere in the MRO.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Box: / def __init__(self, v): self.v = v / def __gt__(self, o): return self.v > o. print(5 < Box(3), 5 < Box(8))
questions.answer: False True. For 5 < Box(...) the int side has no comparison, so Python swaps the operator to the reflected form: it calls Box(value).__gt__(5), evaluating value > 5. For Box(3) that is 3 > 5 = False; for Box(8) it is 8 > 5 = True. This shows __gt__ doing double duty: it is both the > method and the reflected half of < when the right operand is foreign.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Mat: / def __matmul__(self, other): return 'matmul OK'. print(Mat() @ Mat(), Mat() @ 5)
questions.answer: matmul OK matmul OK. The @ operator binds to Matrix.MATMUL semantics and dispatches to parameterized Python object's __matmul__ slot whenever it is defined, regardless of operand types on the right. The array-multiplication semantics of @ come only from user classes; that is why Mat() @ Mat() and Mat() @ 5 both reach the same method and echo the message. This is the operator Python introduced (PEP 465) precisely so matrix types could be polymorphic without overloading *.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Foo: / def __rmatmul__(self, other): return 'rm'. print(2 @ Foo())
questions.answer: rm. 2 is an int, and int defines no __matmul__ (unlike __add__), so the int's slot is missing entirely rather than returning NotImplemented; Python goes straight to the right operand transition. It calls Foo.__rmatmul__(2), other has the value 2, and the method returns 'rm'. This is the reflected variant used when the left operand (or the operator itself) can't handle the right type.

questions.question: Predict the output. class P: / def __pow__(self, o): return f'p({o})'. print(P() ** 2); then evaluate 2 ** P()
questions.answer: p(2) then TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for ** or pow(): 'int' and 'P'. P() ** 2 calls P.__pow__(2) and interpolates it, giving 'p(2)'. For 2 ** P() the int side has no handling, and since P defines no __rpow__, both operands' slots end in NotImplemented, so Python cannot assemble a result and raises the unsupported-operand TypeError. This is standard power fallback: forward __pow__, then reflected __rpow__, then error.

questions.question: Predict the error (fixable bug). class P: / def __pow__(self, other): return 1. What happens with pow(P(), 2, 3)?
questions.answer: TypeError: P.__pow__() takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given. The three-argument built-in pow(x, y, z) is implemented by calling x.__pow__(y, z), passing the modulus as a third positional argument. P.__pow__ only accepts self and other, so Python raises the arity TypeError. Fix: define __pow__(self, other, mod=None) (and optionally __rpow__(self, other, mod=None)) to honor the three-argument form, e.g. return pow(self.v, other, mod).

questions.question: Predict the output. class Idx: / def __index__(self): return 2. l = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]; print(l[Idx()], 'ab' * Idx(), list(range(Idx())))
questions.answer: 30 abab [0, 1]. Every place that needs an integer index or size first consults the __index__ slot: list indexing uses it for the subscript, str.__mul__ (and other sizes) converts via operator.index, and range(Idx()) demands an int index. All three resolve Idx() to the int 2, so the subscript lands on 30, the string repeats twice into 'abab', and the range holds 0, 1. Since Python 3, __index__ (not __int__) is the single source of truth for all integer-entrance contexts.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Idx: / def __index__(self): return 15. print(hex(Idx()))
questions.answer: 0xf. hex() and bin(), oct(), and the format specifiers all convert their argument via the __index__ slot rather than __int__. Idx().__index__ returns 15, which is then rendered in base 16 as 0xf. If __index__ were missing, hex() would raise TypeError instead of silently falling back to __int__.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Twice: / def __int__(self): return 6. print(bool(Twice()))
questions.answer: True. bool() does NOT consult __int__; its conversion order is __bool__, then __len__, then fallback to plain truthy identity semantics. Twice provides none of those, so bool(Twice()) defaults to True even though int(twice) would be 6. This is the classic polymorphism trap: a class that converts cleanly to int is still 'truthy' in an if statement.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Twice: / def __int__(self): return 6. print(int(Twice()))
questions.answer: 6. The int() constructor follows the numeric conversion ladder: try __int__, then __index__ (and __trunc__-style fallbacks for float-related conversions) until an integer is produced. Twice.__int__ returns 6 immediately, so int(Twice()) is 6. This is why __int__ is the right hook for user classes intended to be coerced manually with int(), while slices, len, and indexing insist on __index__ instead.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Odd: / def __getitem__(self, i): / if i > 2: raise IndexError / return 2 * i + 1. print(list(Odd()))
questions.answer: [1, 3, 5]. Odd defines no __iter__, but the iterator protocol has a legacy fallback: if an object lacks __iter__, Python tries the sequence protocol by calling __getitem__ with incrementing integer keys 0, 1, 2, ... until an IndexError is raised. Here key 0 gives 1, key 1 gives 3, key 2 gives 5, and key 3 raises IndexError, ending the iteration. This is duck-typed iteration: no explicit iterator was written, only the subscript-style sequence lookup.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Down: / def __len__(self): return 3 / def __getitem__(self, i): / if 0 <= i < 3: return i + 1 / raise IndexError. print(list(reversed(Down())))
questions.answer: [3, 2, 1]. reversed() has the same duck policy as the iterator fallback: without __reversed__ it uses len() to learn the width, then calls __getitem__ with decreasing indices i = 2, 1, 0 and wraps up when an IndexError surfaces. Down() therefore yields its items backwards. The whole traversal is polymorphic: any object honoring __len__ + __getitem__ becomes reversible with zero extra code.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Both: / def __iter__(self): return iter([9]) / def __getitem__(self, i): return i. print(list(Both()))
questions.answer: [9]. When __iter__ is defined, it completely replaces the legacy __getitem__ iteration path; the subscript-based fallback is only consulted if __iter__ is absent. Both is iterable through its __iter__, which yields a single element 9, so list(Both()) is [9] despite __getitem__ being available. Precedence: modern iterator protocol wins over the old sequence protocol.

questions.question: Predict the error. class OnlyNext: / def __next__(self): return 42. What happens with list(OnlyNext())?
questions.answer: TypeError: 'OnlyNext' object is not iterable. Merely having __next__ does not make an object iterable: the iter() protocol requires __iter__ to return an iterator (an object that itself implements __next__ and returns itself from __iter__), otherwise Python falls back to __getitem__, which is absent here too. So list() can never start consuming it. Fix: add def __iter__(self): return self to make OnlyNext a proper iterator.

questions.question: Predict the output. class FuzzySet: / def __contains__(self, item): return item % 2 == 0. print(2 in FuzzySet(), 3 in FuzzySet())
questions.answer: True False. The in operator dispatches to __contains__ before ever trying iteration: Python asks FuzzySet.__contains__(2) and __contains__(3). The method simply checks parity, so 2 yields True and 3 yields False. This shows how membership polymorphism overrides the default scan behavior; without __contains__, `in` would have fallen back to calling __getitem__/__iter__ and searching element-wise.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Upper(dict): / def __missing__(self, key): return key.upper(). d = Upper(); print(d['hi'], d.get('hi'))
questions.answer: HI None. The __missing__ hook is polymorphic over the mapping protocol: when a dict subclass's __getitem__ fails to find a key, Python invokes d.__missing__(key), whose return value becomes the result of d['hi']; here it uppercases to 'HI'. But d.get('hi') does NOT go through __getitem__, so __missing__ is never called, and the plain .get() returns None. This asymmetry between d[k] and d.get(k) is a classic surprise.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Managed: / def __enter__(self): return 'resource' / def __exit__(self, t, v, tb): print('cleaned up'). with Managed() as r: print(r)
questions.answer:
resource
cleaned up. The with statement is polymorphic over the context-manager protocol: it calls __enter__ and binds its return value to the as variable, and when the block finishes normally it calls __exit__. Here __enter__ returns 'resource', which r prints, and then __exit__ runs at scope exit to print 'cleaned up'. Because the exception triple arrives as (None, None, None) for a clean block, __exit__ can use it to decide whether to swallow errors.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Swallow: / def __enter__(self): return 'ok' / def __exit__(self, t, v, tb): return True. with Swallow(): print(1 / 0) ; print('survived')
questions.answer: survived. The ZeroDivisionError raised inside the block is passed to Swallow.__exit__(ZeroDivisionError, exception, traceback); because __exit__ returns a truthy True, the with machinery treats the exception as handled, suppresses propagation, and execution continues at the following line. Note that 'inside' was never printed because 1 / 0 blew up before the print statement. Returning True from __exit__ is how a context manager deliberately catches and swallows raised exceptions.

questions.question: Predict the output. class NonData: / def __get__(self, obj, typ=None): return 'PROXY'. class C: x = NonData(). c = C(); c.x = 'local'; print(c.x)
questions.answer: local. NonData is a non-data descriptor, i.e. it defines __get__ but no __set__ (or __delete__). During lookup, an instance-__dict__ entry takes priority over a non-data descriptor, so c.x='local' shadows the class-level descriptor and reads back 'local'. This is the exact mechanism behind method binding vs attribute assignment: ordinary functions are non-data descriptors, so assigning self.method = x works.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Data: / def __get__(self, obj, typ=None): return 'PROXY' / def __set__(self, obj, value): obj.__dict__['x'] = value. class D: x = Data(). d = D(); d.x = 'local'; print(d.x, d.__dict__['x'])
questions.answer: PROXY local. Data is a data descriptor (it owns both __get__ and __set__), and data descriptors take precedence over the instance dictionary on every access. So d.x always routes through Data.__get__, which abandons the stored value and returns 'PROXY'; the assignment d.x='local' still fires __set__, which parks 'local' inside d.__dict__['x']. This is the descriptor-precedence rule that makes property/slots work: the __set__ presence flips normal attribute-shadowing behavior.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Field: / def __set_name__(self, owner, name): self.name = '_' + name / def __get__(self, obj, typ=None): / return self.name if obj is None else getattr(obj, self.name, None) / def __set__(self, obj, value): setattr(obj, self.name, value). class User: name = Field() / def __init__(self, n): self.name = n. u = User('ann'); print(u.name, u._name, User.name)
questions.answer: ann ann _name. When the class is created, Python calls __set_name__ on each descriptor with the class and the attribute name, so the Field learns it is called 'name' and stores '_name' as its backing key. u.name = 'ann' routes through __set__ and writes u._name = 'ann', so both u.name and u._name are 'ann'. Accessing User.name on the class (obj is None) hits the guarded branch and returns the stored descriptor label '_name'. __set_name__ is how descriptors become attribute-name-aware without hardcoding field names.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Color: / def __init__(self, c): self.c = c / def __eq__(self, o): return isinstance(o, Color) and self.c == o.c / def __hash__(self): return hash(self.c). d = {Color('red'): 'hot'}; print(d[Color('red')])
questions.answer: hot. The dict uses the hash to find the bucket, then calls == to confirm equality of the probe key with each candidate inside that bucket. Color('red') hashes identically — hash('red') — and Color.__eq__ compares the payload strings, so the lookup matches the stored key and returns 'hot'. This is polymorphic key hashing: any class that agrees on hash and eq can serve as a dictionary key.

questions.question: Predict the error. class E: / def __eq__(self, o): return True. try: {E(): 1} except TypeError as e: print(e). Why?
questions.answer: TypeError: cannot use 'E' as a dict key (unhashable type: 'E'). Merely defining __eq__ installs __hash__ = None on the class, because Python assumes eq-able objects that did not opt in to hashing should not be hashable. Since E never redefines __hash__, its instances have no hash function and cannot enter a dict or set. The fix is to define __hash__ as well; the two must stay consistent.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Maybe: / def __init__(self, i): self.i = i / def __eq__(self, o): return True / def __hash__(self): return self.i. d = {Maybe(1): 'A'}; print(d.get(Maybe(2)), d.get(Maybe(1)))
questions.answer: None A. The stored key hashes to 1, so it lives in bucket 1. Looking up Maybe(2) hashes to 2, lands in bucket 2, finds nothing there, and returns None even though Maybe(1) == Maybe(2) would be True: the dict never compares objects in different buckets. Maybe(1) searches bucket 1, collides on the equal/hash-matched entry, and returns 'A'. This demonstrates why __hash__ and __eq__ must be mutually consistent, or dict lookups silently break.

questions.question: Predict the output. import collections.abc as abc. class Rounded: / def __len__(self): return 4 / def __getitem__(self, i): return i. abc.Sequence.register(Rounded); print(isinstance(Rounded(), abc.Sequence))
questions.answer: True. isinstance check is polymorphic through ABC registration: abc.Sequence.register(Rounded) declares Rounded a virtual subclass with zero code changes, so isinstance(Rounded(), abc.Sequence) returns True even though Rounded never inherits from the ABC. The check is satisfied by the registration table rather than the MRO. (The same would be true for issubclass.) This is how third-party types retroactively present as 'sequences' to generic functions guarded by isinstance.

questions.question: Predict the output. import collections.abc as abc. class Iter: / def __iter__(self): return iter(()). print(isinstance(Iter(), abc.Iterable)). Explain why no register() is needed.
questions.answer: True. collections.abc.Iterable defines __subclasshook__, an alternative to registration: when the normal MRO check fails, C implementation of isinstance consults the ABC's __subclasshook__ method, which here inspects the actual structure of the candidate and sees the __iter__ method. Since Iter implements __iter__, the hook returns True, so isinstance succeeds without any isinstance/register call. This is structural (duck-typed) polymorphism built into the ABC machinery.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Animal: pass. class Cat(Animal): pass. for k in (Cat(), Animal(), 'x'): print(type(k) is Animal, isinstance(k, Animal))
questions.answer:
False True
True True
False False. type(k) is Animal requires the exact, identical type object, so Cat() fails that identity check (False) while Animal() passes. isinstance(k, Animal) is polymorphic: it accepts Cat instances, Animal instances, and their subclasses as instances of Animal, so the first two lines end True; the string 'x' shares no relation, giving False False. The lesson: isinstance is the polymorphic test, type() is the exact-match test, and reachable code should prefer isinstance.

questions.question: Predict the output. class A: pass. class B(A): pass. class C(A): pass. class D(B, C): pass. print(D.__mro__)
questions.answer: (<class '__main__.D'>, <class '__main__.B'>, <class '__main__.C'>, <class '__main__.A'>, <class 'object'>). The C3 linearization for the diamond D(B, C) merges the base lists into D, B, C, A, object, guaranteeing that each class appears after all its direct bases and that the ordering respects the left-to-right base tuple. This exact MRO is what super() walks: starting at D, super() positions land on the next class down this list. Method resolution is then a sequential scan of the MRO.

questions.question: Predict the output. class A: def m(self): print('A', end=''). class B(A): def m(self): super().m(); print('B', end=''). class C(A): def m(self): super().m(); print('C', end=''). class D(B, C): pass. D().m()
questions.answer: ACB. D has no m, so B.m runs first; B's super() no longer means 'A' directly, it means 'the next class in D's MRO after B', which is C. C.m then calls super() which, next in the MRO, is A, printing A first, then C prints, then B prints: ACB. This is super() cooperation: linearization plus super() chaining produces exactly one call to each method along the full diamond, and A is visited only once.

questions.question: Predict the error. class X: pass. class Y: pass. class Z(X, Y): pass. class W(Y, X): pass. class V(Z, W): pass. What is raised when defining V?
questions.answer: TypeError: Cannot create a consistent method resolution order (MRO) for bases X, Y. Z(X, Y) demands X before Y while W(Y, X) demands Y before X; merging them for V(Z, W) would require X ahead of Y (from Z's list) and Y ahead of X (from W's list) at the same time. C3 cannot linearize such a conflict as a topological order, so Python refuses to build the class. This is what happens when two parallel inheritance branches impose contradictory base orderings.

questions.question: Predict the error. def make_sound(animal): return animal.speak(). What happens with make_sound(['list']) — why is the failure at call time?
questions.answer: AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'speak'. Nothing is checked when make_sound is defined or when the list is passed in; the method resolution for .speak happens lazily inside the function body at the exact moment of the attribute access. Python looks up 'speak' on list's class and its bases, finds nothing, and only then raises AttributeError. This lazy lookup is duck typing's pitfall: any object may be handed to the function, and correctness is verified the moment the real method is needed.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Proxy: / def __init__(self, obj): self._obj = obj / def __getattr__(self, name): return getattr(self._obj, name). class Greeter: / def hi(self): return 'hello' / def bye(self): return 'goodbye'. p = Proxy(Greeter()); print(p.hi(), p.bye())
questions.answer: hello goodbye. __getattr__ runs only when normal attribute lookup fails, so p.hi first searches Proxy for 'hi', finds none, and falls into __getattr__('hi'), which forwards getattr(self._obj, 'hi') to the wrapped Greeter. Both hi and bye are resolved by delegation, letting the Proxy polymorphically stand in for whatever object it wraps. Note that self._obj is reachable directly because it lives in the instance dict, so __getattr__ never swallows it.

questions.question: Find the bug. class Bad: / def __getattr__(self, name): return self.missing. What happens when you evaluate Bad().anything?
questions.answer: RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded. Accessing Bad().anything fails normal lookup and calls Bad.__getattr__('anything'), whose body then accesses self.missing; 'missing' is not in the instance dict, so lookup fails again and re-enters __getattr__. Each recursion spins back into the same method until the interpreter exhausts its guard and raises RecursionError. Fix: guard the fallback, e.g. if name == 'missing': return None, or consult self.__dict__, or raise AttributeError instead of recursing.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Tracer: / def __getattribute__(self, name): print('GET', name); return super().__getattribute__(name). t = Tracer(); t.x = 1; print(t.x)
questions.answer:
GET x
1. __getattribute__ is invoked for EVERY attribute access, even successful ones, so t.x triggers it, prints 'GET x', and delegates to super().__getattribute__ to get the stored 1. Unlike __getattr__, which only runs on failures, __getattribute__ is the unconditional hook. If the method forgets to call super(), every read — including reads of internal state — will fail or recurse.

questions.question: Predict the output. class CountDown: / def __init__(self, n): self.n = n / def __call__(self): self.n -= 1; return self.n. c = CountDown(3); print(c(), c(), c())
questions.answer: 2 1 0. Defining __call__ turns CountDown instances into callable objects: invoking c() dispatches to c.__call__(), which decrements and returns the new n. Each call mutates shared state, so the three calls emit 2, then 1, then 0. This callable-object polymorphism is what closures and functors use to bundle behavior plus state in a single callable entity.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Printer: / def __init__(self, fmt): self.format = fmt. def upper(s): return s.upper(). def lower(s): return s.lower(). print(Printer(upper).format('hi'), Printer(lower).format('hi'))
questions.answer: HI hi. Polymorphism here is exercised through stored functions: Printer stores whichever callable was injected in its constructor, and calling .format('hi') dispatches to that function. Printer(upper) formats to 'HI' while Printer(lower) formats to 'hi', the same API yielding different behavior. This strategy-pattern style achieves polymorphism without subclasses — any callable object works, since Python functions are ordinary first-class attributes.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Money: / def __init__(self, v): self.v = v / def __format__(self, spec): return f'{self.v}{spec} credits'. print(f'{Money(42):}'); print(format(Money(42), 'X'))
questions.answer:
42 credits
42X credits. The f-string and format() both hand their format specification to Money.__format__(spec): the empty spec (f'{...:}') yields '42 credits', while spec 'X' is appended verbatim to the value, producing '42X credits'. __format__ is the polymorphic hook that lets every class define how it renders inside f-strings and format(). Without it, f'{obj}' would fall back to str(obj) instead.
